passages.t: A wise son, an honest harvest, and the righteous remembered
passages.happening:
A new heading opens the book's largest collection: “The proverbs of Solomon” (verse 1). The first saying picks up the family of chapters 1 to 9: ‘A wise son brings joy to his father, but a foolish son grief to his mother’ (verse 1).

Then come sayings about money and work. ‘Ill-gotten treasures profit nothing, but righteousness brings deliverance from death’ (verse 2). ‘The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry, but He denies the craving of the wicked’ (verse 3). ‘Idle hands make one poor, but diligent hands bring wealth’ (verse 4). ‘He who gathers in summer is a wise son, but he who sleeps during harvest is a disgraceful son’ (verse 5).

And sayings about a good name. ‘The memory of the righteous is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot’ (verse 7). ‘He who walks in integrity walks securely, but he who perverts his ways will be found out’ (verse 9). ‘The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The long poems are over. The father has made his appeal, and now he hands his son the contents of Wisdom's house: hundreds of short sayings to be learned by heart and turned over in real life. From here to 22:16 the book moves in small pieces, not one argument. The reader's task changes from following a speech to pondering one saying at a time.

Almost every saying has two lines joined by ‘but’, the second saying the same truth from the other side. The righteous, tsaddiq, and the wicked, rasha, appear more than any other pair. Sayings are also linked by repeated words. Verses 6 and 11 end with the very same line.

Harvest was life or death. Grain came in late spring and early summer, fruit through the summer, and a family's survival through the winter rains depended on getting it in on time. A son who slept through harvest put the whole household at risk.

Honor and shame were public. A person lived on in the memory of the town, so to be remembered with disgust, a name that rots, was a kind of second death.
passages.later: The psalms say the same of the righteous: ‘Surely he will never be shaken; the righteous man will be remembered forever’ (Psalm 112:6). And the psalmist warns about trusting in what verse 2 calls ill-gotten treasures: ‘They trust in their wealth and boast in their great riches’ (Psalm 49:6).
passages.asks: The chapter begins with a son who brings joy or grief to his parents. Ask whom your choices bring joy or grief to. And ask what name you are building, the kind that is remembered gladly or the kind that rots.

passages.t: Love covers, and words are many
passages.happening:
‘Hatred stirs up dissension, but love covers all transgressions’ (verse 12).

Many of these sayings are about speech. ‘Wisdom is found on the lips of the discerning’ (verse 13). ‘The wise store up knowledge, but the mouth of the fool invites destruction’ (verse 14). ‘The one who conceals hatred has lying lips, and whoever spreads slander is a fool’ (verse 18). “When words are many, sin is unavoidable, but he who restrains his lips is wise” (verse 19). ‘The tongue of the righteous is choice silver’ (verse 20), and ‘The lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for lack of judgment’ (verse 21).

Among them are sayings on money and correction. ‘The wealth of the rich man is his fortified city, but poverty is the ruin of the poor’ (verse 15). ‘Whoever heeds instruction is on the path to life, but he who ignores reproof goes astray’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
In a world with few written records, a person's word was contract, testimony and reputation all at once. Instruction happened at meals, in the fields and at the city gate, all by word of mouth. That is why the book gives so much attention to lips and tongue.

Cover is kasah, to conceal or cover over. Love does not expose and spread every wrong. It does not mean pretending nothing happened. It means refusing to keep stirring up a quarrel.

Verse 15 is an observation, not praise. Money can be a rich man's fortress, and poverty can leave the poor with no walls at all. The book reports that hard fact and, as later sayings show, it puts God on the side of the poor.

Verse 19 is plain advice for anyone who talks a great deal: the more words, the more chances to sin.
passages.later: Peter echoes verse 12: ‘love covers over a multitude of sins’ (1 Peter 4:8). James says the same of the tongue as verse 19: ‘We all stumble in many ways. If anyone is never at fault in what he says, he is a perfect man’ (James 3:2).
passages.asks: Love covers, hatred stirs up. Ask whether there is an old wrong you keep bringing back up. And ask where in your speech this week fewer words would have been wiser.

passages.t: The righteous secure, and a hard question
passages.happening:
‘The blessing of the LORD enriches, and He adds no sorrow to it’ (verse 22). ‘The fool delights in shameful conduct, but a man of understanding has wisdom’ (verse 23).

‘When the whirlwind passes, the wicked are no more, but the righteous are secure forever’ (verse 25). The slacker is to his employer ‘Like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes’ (verse 26).

‘The fear of the LORD prolongs life, but the years of the wicked will be cut short’ (verse 27). ‘The hope of the righteous is joy’ (verse 28). ‘The way of the LORD is a refuge to the upright’ (verse 29). ‘The righteous will never be shaken, but the wicked will not inhabit the land’ (verse 30). The chapter ends with speech again: ‘The lips of the righteous know what is fitting, but the mouth of the wicked is perverse’ (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
The LORD's name comes four times in this chapter. Israel's neighbors had collections of wise sayings too, and Israel shares their form. But it roots its sayings in the LORD.

Verses 27 to 30 gather sayings on how lasting the life of the righteous is. The whirlwind of verse 25 is a sudden storm that flattens what is not built to last. The righteous are compared to something that stands when it passes.

Verse 26 is one of the book's sharp, funny pictures. Vinegar sets the teeth on edge, and smoke stings the eyes. Sending a slacker on an errand feels just like that.
passages.later: The psalms say it this way: ‘Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion. It cannot be moved; it abides forever’ (Psalm 125:1). But Ecclesiastes also records what it saw: ‘A righteous man perishing in his righteousness, and a wicked man living long in his wickedness’ (Ecclesiastes 7:15).
passages.hard:
Are these sayings promises? Don't the righteous sometimes go hungry and die young?

Read as guarantees, verses like 3, 27 and 30 would simply be false, and the Bible knows it. Job is a righteous man who loses everything. Ecclesiastes says ‘The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong’ (Ecclesiastes 9:11), and that the righteous sometimes perish in their righteousness. Many psalms cry out because the wicked prosper.

The answer is in what a proverb is. It describes how life usually goes in a world God has ordered: hard work tends toward plenty, dishonesty tends toward ruin, a name for integrity tends to last. It is a true pattern, not a contract with a date attached. Proverbs itself shows this when it later sets two opposite sayings side by side (26:4-5) and leaves the reader to judge which one fits.

Some interpreters add that many sayings look past the present to the final outcome, since the righteous are secure ‘forever’ (verse 25) in a way that death does not cancel. Others stress that Proverbs speaks mainly of this life and leaves the exceptions to Job and Ecclesiastes. Either way, these sayings are wisdom to live by, not formulas to hold God to, and they give no one a reason to think that someone who is hungry or grieving must have deserved it.
passages.asks: The book says the way of the LORD is a refuge. Ask what you run to when the storm comes. And ask whether you have ever treated a proverb as a promise God owed you, and what changes if you read it as wisdom instead.
